abstract: The October 14, 2026 update to the Yale Budget Lab's AI labor market tracker, incorporating September 2026 CPS microdata and the first third-quarter 2026 synthetic difference-in-differences estimates. It still finds no clear evidence of AI-related labor market disruption in occupational churn, employment or wages, but for the first time its headline flags a counter-signal: unemployment among AI-exposed workers has tended to grow faster than among comparable unexposed workers since late 2022, including in Q3 2026, though the estimates are volatile and not statistically distinguishable from zero this quarter. It remains the main CPS-based counterweight to payroll-based findings of early-career displacement.
keyFindings: Updated to September 2026 CPS microdata, the analysis 'does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI'; churn and employment and wage comparisons are 'not consistent with any large-scale disruption to date.'

The SDID unemployment estimate for AI-exposed versus synthetic unexposed occupations is 1.14 in 2026Q3 (95% CI -0.19 to 2.48) and has been positive every quarter since 2024Q3; its confidence interval excluded zero in 2023Q2, 2023Q3, 2025Q2 and 2025Q3 but not in 2026Q3. Yale calls the estimates 'volatile' and says they should be interpreted cautiously.
SDID employment-share (0.0015, CI -0.0059 to 0.0089) and real-wage (-0.0050, CI -0.047 to 0.036) estimates for 2026Q3 are centred near zero.

Occupational dissimilarity from the November 2022 baseline reached 5.56 points by September 2026, slightly above the computer (4.49), internet (4.75) and 2016 control (4.97) windows at the same horizon but within the 2021-2022 baselines (5.22-5.60).
The share of workers in the highest AI-exposure group is 18.3 percent, essentially unchanged from 18.2 percent at ChatGPT's launch.

Among the long-term unemployed (27+ weeks), the share from the highest-exposure group rose from 14.7 percent in November 2022 to 19.5 percent in September 2026, while among the newly unemployed (<5 weeks) it fell from 12.7 to 11.5 percent; Yale's summary does not discuss this.
Usage-based measures are flat: 69.7 percent of observed AI usage is automation-type and 76.8 percent of workers are in automation-dominant occupations, versus 69.6 and 76.0 percent in November 2022.
methodology: Current Population Survey microdata (via IPUMS) analyzed three ways: occupational dissimilarity indices on 12-month moving averages, benchmarked against computer, internet and control-period baselines; AI-exposure and Anthropic usage metrics applied to employed and unemployed workers by unemployment duration (three-month moving averages; Eloundou et al. GPT-beta exposure); and a synthetic difference-in-differences comparison of AI-exposed against synthetic unexposed occupations with treatment in 2022Q4 and confidence intervals per Clarke et al. (2022). Monthly tabs update with each CPS release; the SDID comparisons update quarterly. Published as an interactive tool whose data are served as CSVs alongside a manifest; methodology in Gimbel et al. (2025), Gimbel, Kendall and Kulsakdinun (2026), and Gimbel, Kendall and Nunn (2026).
qualifiers: Still mainly a null result, and CPS cells are too small to detect effects concentrated in narrow occupations or one age band, where payroll and posting data locate the signal. The SDID outcome units are per-occupation averages (employment share of population, log unemployment rate) and the publisher's axis labels do not map cleanly onto them; they are not shares of US jobs and should not be converted into one. The unemployment signal is the first headline caveat in the series, but it is volatile quarter to quarter (0.14 in 2026Q2, 1.14 in 2026Q3) and the authors note it is not accompanied by other indications of labor market impact. Exposure indices assign exposure by task content, and the usage metrics rely on a fixed Anthropic snapshot, so their movement reflects only occupational mix.
